_meta: A per-layer gradient multiplier on the residual path and a set of network depths, used to show why placing the LayerNorm INSIDE the residual branch (pre-norm) keeps a clean identity path so gradients survive depth, while placing it ON the residual stream (post-norm, the original Transformer) attenuates the gradient at every layer and makes deep training unstable. A transformer layer combines a sublayer (attention or MLP) with a residual connection and a normalization. There are two orders. Post-norm, the original Transformer design, computes x = LayerNorm(x + sublayer(x)): the normalization sits on the main residual stream, so on the backward pass the gradient flowing toward earlier layers passes through the norm's Jacobian at every layer, which scales it by a factor typically below 1 -- so the gradient reaching the first layers shrinks as depth grows (a vanishing-gradient effect), and training deep post-norm transformers is unstable and needs careful learning-rate warmup. Pre-norm computes x = x + sublayer(LayerNorm(x)): the normalization is inside the branch, and the residual stream itself is a pure identity path from input to output, so the gradient flows back along that path undiminished -- the multiplier on the residual path is exactly 1 regardless of depth, and deep pre-norm transformers train stably. The difference is entirely where the norm sits relative to the residual add. residual_multiplier gives each variant's per-layer gradient multiplier on the residual path (pre-norm keeps the identity path at 1.0; post-norm's norm attenuates, modeled here at 0.85); depths are the network depths to evaluate; vanish_threshold is the gradient magnitude below which the signal is considered vanished. These are the fixture; the input-gradient magnitude of each variant at each depth, and whether it has vanished, are computed.
